article_text:
Japan’s production committee system, in which a group of companies jointly finance a film and share its rights, has helped spread risk across the industry. But it can also cap budgets at what the industry itself can raise, make it harder for overseas investors to take part and slow decisions when every rights holder must agree.

At a panel at TIFFCOM , the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival , speakers examined whether film funds can ease those limits while still fitting Japan’s market.

“Film Funds in Japan: What Works, What Doesn’t, and What Comes Next” featured Kii Muneyuki, CEO and producer of K2 Pictures, which works with filmmakers including Kore-eda Hirokazu , Miike Takashi and Nishikawa Miwa; Ibe Tomonobu, CEO of Questry, a Tokyo startup that uses digital securities to fund anime and other Japanese content; Nakagawa Keita, managing director at MUFG Bank; and Motoyanagi Yusuke, partner at law firm Nishimura & Asahi.

Kii presented K2P Film Fund I as one example of a new structure. The fund closed in February at about JPY5 billion ($32 million) and aims to back around 50 films over seven years. It is a blind pool, meaning investors commit money before the films are chosen. Its investors include MUFG, the Development Bank of Japan and other financial institutions and companies, and a greenlight committee oversees project approvals. Kii said five films had been released in theaters in 2026.

Kii said a central question for film funds is how to return revenue to creators, including income from streaming and other windows after a film’s theatrical run. He also said it is hard to rely on overseas box office, and that Japanese companies need to build businesses beyond distribution.

The panel compared financing structures in the U.S. and South Korea. In the U.S., producers combine presales with completion guarantees to help secure bank loans. A completion guarantee covers delivery of a film on budget and on schedule, rather than its commercial performance. South Korea relies on public-private support, with government-backed guarantees helping projects get bank financing.

Nakagawa presented a Japan-specific feasibility study commissioned by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. MUFG was selected to carry it out on March 31. Running through February 2027, the study will use real-world data to develop valuation and completion-guarantee models, and test the full process from application and review to contract drafting. The study assesses feasibility and does not guarantee that financing or completion guarantees will become available.

The discussion closed with four priorities: regulation, capital, creators and cross-border business. These include clarifying which regulations should be expanded and when, combining debt with subsidies and completion guarantees, and building creator returns into fund structures. Speakers also pointed to language and tax hurdles to cross-border investment, including “permanent establishment” rules that can make international investors liable for Japanese tax.

article_text:
The year of unlikely box office smashes continues as “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” opened to a thunderous $31.6 million, shattering records to become the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film in history. It easily toppled the previous benchmark established in 2002 by the wuxia epic “Hero,” which kicked off with $17.8 million. Globally, “Godzilla Minus Zero’s” haul stands at $63 million.

And it comes on the heels of a string of films that have defied conventional wisdom to resonate with moviegoers. Yes, the box office is still dominated by sequels and comic book movies like “Toy Story 5” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but there’s been a lot more variety. Audiences have turned out in force for an original sci-fi adventure (“Project Hail Mary,” $684.6 million worldwide); a pair of low-budget horror films from 20-something auteurs with YouTube pedigree (“Obsession,” $524.3 million worldwide; “Backrooms,” $400.6 million worldwide); an adaptation of a Greek epic we were all forced to read in school (“The Odyssey,” $1.8 billion worldwide), and a three-hour documentary about a Silicon Valley cheat (“You Can See Everything,” $73.7 million and counting). Clearly, people are looking for something different.

In the case of “Godzilla Minus Zero,” it helped that the first film, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” was an unexpected sleeper hit, grossing an impressive $57.1 million. But the first “Godzilla” opened to a mere $11.4 million, showing that the audience for the first monster movie grew on home entertainment. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is poised to bypass its predecessor to become the highest-grossing live-action Japanese movie in history. Once again, the film was directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also worked on the special effects, produced by Japan’s Tojo, and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

The success of “Godzilla Minus Zero” also demonstrates that subtitles are no barrier to box office success, something that Netflix and other streamers discovered with the popularity of local-language programming like “Squid Game,” “Money Heist,” and “Lupin.” The story at multiplexes is no different. U.S. audiences have filled auditoriums to watch “Parasite” ($53.8 million domestic), “Ne Zha 2” ($23.2 million domestic), and “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle” ($136.9 million domestic). The outsized grosses for “Godzilla Minus Zero” probably mean we haven’t heard the last of the fire-breathing Kaiju.

The monster movie made quick work of its main competition, Warner Bros. Animation’s “ The Cat in the Hat ,” which stumbled with $20 million domestically and $30 million globally. The family film cost $92 million to produce and extends a string of misses for Warner Bros., which was recently purchased by Skydance. Insiders say that the studio has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on bombs like “Digger,” “Supergirl,” and “The Bride!” and “The Cat in the Hat” won’t do much to mop up all that red ink.

On October 23, Chanel is dropping the second volume of Arts & Culture , its free 300-page magazine, graced with new photographs by Cindy Sherman , wearing — you might have guessed— Chanel. More like raw, unsewn Chanel, in the form of their archival fabrics that Sherman draped and wrapped around herself. As Vanity Fair reported, the brand sent Sherman rolls of vintage fabric to do with what she pleased. “I said, ‘Well, is it okay if I cut things up, cut holes into them and whatnot?’” Sherman told Vanity Fair . Yes, Chanel was very much ok with it, and just like that , the fashion brand had direct, exclusive access to Sherman’s latest series of photographs, titled “Fabric Matrons,” which will also be shown at Hauser & Wirth ’s Mayfair gallery during Frieze London . From the looks of a few photos published in Vanity Fair , it does seem like Sherman effectively played dress-up, cutting poncho-style holes in a whole lot of Chanel tweeds, and not to an unflattering or ridiculous effect. To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter .

Good morning!

Cindy Sherman is the cover star of the second volume of Chanel’s Arts & Culture magazine.

Austrian presidential candidate Gunther Fehlinger-Jahn says that if elected, he’ll return a 16th-century Aztec headdress to Mexico, currently located in Vienna’s Weltmuseum.

A descendant of the 19th-century artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu is taking legal action to demand the removal of Marc Chagall’s painting on the ceiling of the Palais Garnier opera house.

The Headlines

SHERMAN IN CHANEL TWEED . On October 23, Chanel is dropping the second volume of Arts & Culture , its free 300-page magazine, graced with new photographs by Cindy Sherman , wearing — you might have guessed— Chanel. More like raw, unsewn Chanel, in the form of their archival fabrics that Sherman draped and wrapped around herself. As Vanity Fair reported, the brand sent Sherman rolls of vintage fabric to do with what she pleased. “I said, ‘Well, is it okay if I cut things up, cut holes into them and whatnot?’” Sherman told Vanity Fair . Yes, Chanel was very much ok with it, and just like that , the fashion brand had direct, exclusive access to Sherman’s latest series of photographs, titled “Fabric Matrons,” which will also be shown at Hauser & Wirth ’s Mayfair gallery during Frieze London . From the looks of a few photos published in Vanity Fair , it does seem like Sherman effectively played dress-up, cutting poncho-style holes in a whole lot of Chanel tweeds, and not to an unflattering or ridiculous effect. Sherman’s characters appear thoughtful, if solemn, as though weighed down by experience, draped in glamorous, bejeweled get-ups. “At one point I remember writing in my journal, ‘Who the fuck wants to look at pictures of old ladies anyway?’” Sherman said. I guess we’re about to find out. RUFFLED FEATHERS . Austrian presidential candidate Gunther Fehlinger-Jahn says that if elected, he’ll return a 16th-century feathered Aztec headdress to Mexico, currently in Vienna’s Weltmuseum , reports The Art Newspaper . For decades, the Mexican government has been requesting the return of the 4½ -foot-high and 5¾ -foot-wide, ornate Quetzal headdress, or quetzalapanecayotl , that once belonged to Aztec ruler Moctezuma, though it is believed he never wore it. It’s unclear how the artifact left Mexico in the first place. “Austria and Mexico should negotiate a bilateral solution based on friendship rather than confrontation,” Fehlinger-Jahn said. In 2020, Mexico requested to borrow the headdress for an exhibition, but Austrian officials refused to do so, citing the object’s fragility as the reason.

The Digest

A descendant of the 19th-century classical artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu is taking legal action to demand the removal of Marc Chagall ’s iconic painting on the ceiling of the Palais Garnier opera house in Paris, because it covers an original oil on copper fresco by Lenepveu. [ The Guardian ]

In March 2027, French Galerie Christophe Gaillard is opening a new space in Bangkok, inside the Bangkok Kunsthalle . [ The Art Newspaper, France ]

A decade and a half after Amy Winehouse ’s death, her life is still being explored — even excavated — in a new exhibition full of simulacra of the singer’s personal items by artist Alex Margo Arden , titled “Nothing Personal,” on view through January 23. [ ARTnews ]

Two stolen Auguste Renoir paintings were recovered in “record time,” and are currently being examined for any damage by conservation experts, before their planned return to the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, according to France’s ministry of culture. [ press release ]

A Welsh medieval myth claiming that the Roman emperor Magnus Maximus set up a military camp near Frenni Fawr in Wales has just been backed by archeological evidence. [ The Guardian ]

The Kicker

A RADICAL WELCOME. Zoë Ryan , director of the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles, recently discussed how she plans to steer the museum into the next era and make it an anchoring focal point of the Westside Los Angeles arts district, reports the Los Angeles Times . For one, she is working to raise the profile of educational projects, including professional training for teachers who bring arts curricula to classrooms. Overlooked women artists are also a top priority, as shown with two major fall surveys of artists Huguette Caland and Mavis Pusey . Among other “bold projects,” Ryan wants to host a ground-floor room for artmaking, reading, and study, called the Nook, which she views as a “radical welcome.”

article_text:
Die aktuelle Shortlist des Young Generation Art Award steht fest. Fünf Künstlerinnen und Künstler gehen für die dritte Runde der Auszeichnung ins Rennen. Der Preis wurde von Degussa Goldhandel in Kooperation mit Monopol ins Leben gerufen. Er fördert vielversprechende junge Positionen in der zeitgenössischen Kunst.

Hope Bartley, Joanna Chia-yu Lin, Pierre-Yves Delannoy, Joana Loewis und Louisa Pieper sind für den Young Generation Art Award 2027 nominiert. Die neue Shortlist wurde zur Eröffnung der Frieze London auf der Messe vorgestellt. Dort ist noch bis Sonntag in der Degussa-Lounge eine große Ausstellung des Young Generation Art Award-Preisträgers Ken Nwadiogbu zu sehen, dessen Werk die Jury 2026 überzeugte.

Der Young Generation Art Award fördert Künstlerinnen und Künstler bis zu einem Alter von 35 Jahren. Das Interesse an dem Preis ist groß: Beim Open Call zum Preis gingen in diesem Jahr knapp 600 Bewerbungen internationaler Künstlerinnen und Künstler ein.

Die fünf ausgewählten Künstlerinnen und Künstler werden im Novemberheft des Monopol Magazins vorgestellt. Ab dem 27. November sind ihre Arbeiten in einer gemeinsamen Ausstellung in der Degussa-Niederlassung in Berlin, Französische Straße 48, zu sehen.

„Unser Ziel ist es, den Dialog zwischen zeitgenössischer Kunst, Sammlern und der Öffentlichkeit aktiv zu fördern . Indem wir diesen außergewöhnlichen jungen Nachwuchskünstlerinnen und -künstlern eine Bühne bieten, machen wir ihre Werke auch einem internationalen Fachpublikum zugänglich,“ so Alexander Betz, CEO der Degussa Group.

Elke Buhr, Chefredakteurin von Monopol, sagt: „Die vielen Bewerbungen für diesen Jahrgang des Young Generation Art Awards hatten ein hervorragendes Niveau und zeigen die Qualität und Vielfalt der jungen Kunst. Ich freue mich, dass der Preis sich in nur drei Jahren bereits so gut etablieren konnte.“

Der Young Generation Art Award ist mit 10.000 Euro für den ersten Preis dotiert; jede Nominierung für die Shortlist wird zusätzlich mit 3000 Euro ausgezeichnet. Eine Fachjury wählt aus den fünf Finalistinnen und Finalisten die Gewinnerin oder den Gewinner 2027 aus. Sie besteht aus Yilmaz Dziewior, Direktor des Museum Ludwig in Köln, der Kuratorin Maya Heckelmann sowie Elke Buhr, Chefredakteurin von Monopol. Die Preisverleihung erfolgt Anfang 2027.

Kurzbiografien der Nominierten

Hope Bartley (geb. 1993 in Kingston, Jamaica) studierte an der Caribbean School of Architecture in Jamaica und am Bauhaus Dessau. Er lebt und arbeitet in München.

Joanna Chia-yu Lin (geb. 1995 in Taiwan) studierte Kunst in Taipei und an der Oslo National Academy of Fine Arts in Norwegen. Sie lebt und arbeitet in Norwegen und Taiwan.

Pierre-Yves Delannoy (geb. 1995 in Châlons-sur-Marne, Frankreich) studierte Kunst und Architektur in Paris, Versailles und München. Er schloss sein Studium 2025 als Meisterschüler von Julian Rosefeldt an der Kunstakademie München ab. Er lebt und arbeitet in München.

Joana Loewis (geb. 1996) studierte an der Kunstakademie München und schloss 2026 als Meisterschülerin von Gregor Hildebrandt ab. Sie lebt und arbeitet südlich von München.

Louisa Pieper (geb. 1997 in Deutschland) studierte an der Burg Giebichenstein in Halle und der Hochschule für Grafik und Buchkunst in Leipzig. Sie lebt und arbeitet in Leipzig.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: The Station , the debut narrative feature from Yemeni-Scottish filmmaker Sara Ishaq, has been picked up for North America by Watermelon Pictures .

Watermelon will release the film theatrically later this year.

The Station debuted in the Critics’ Week competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. The official synopsis reads: Set against the backdrop of war-torn Yemen, The Station follows Layal, who runs a women-only petrol station where the rules are simple: no men, no weapons, no politics. A rare sanctuary of safety and solidarity, the station becomes a vibrant gathering place where women from every walk of life come together with humor, resilience, and hope. When Layal’s younger brother faces forced enlistment, she reunites with her estranged sister to save the one life they still can, embarking on an emotional journey that balances warmth, wit, and quiet defiance in the face of extraordinary circumstances.

The film was produced by Screen Project and Georges Films, and co-produced by One Two Films, KeplerFilm, Barentsfilm, Setara Films, The Imaginarium Films, and ZDF Das kleine Fernsehspiel – ARTE. Jon Kilik ( Babel ) serves as executive producer.

“ I couldn’t think of better hands to entrust our film to in the US than Watermelon Pictures,” Ishaq said in a statement.

“Yemen so often makes US headlines in the most negative light, while the spirit and humanity of its people remain largely unknown to the American public. Watermelon Pictures understands what it means to humanize our narratives and bring them to audiences who rarely get to see us on our own terms.”

article_text:
Earlier this month at the Metropolitan Museum of Art , the three artists chosen for the Artisan Residency Programme, a collaboration between the museum and Vacheron Constantin, unveiled the works that each has created through the program.

The Swiss luxury watch company launched the 18-month residency program with the Met in May 2025, making the third such partnership for the company. (The company also has partnerships with the Louvre, dating to 2019, and the Palace Museum in Beijing, established in 2024.)

The program is meant to pass on, preserve, and reinterpret traditional craft techniques. As part of the program, artists spent considerable time at both the Met and the Vacheron Constantin Manufacture in Geneva, and then used those experiences as launching points for their own works. The three artists selected were Aspen Golann, Ibrahim Said, and Joy Harvey.

For the residency, Golann produced a monumental wooden vessel adorned with nature motifs carved in bas relief. For the piece she drew inspiration from a series of wooden chests from the 17th to the 19th century in Connecticut and Pennsylvania. Those works and other similar ones in the Met’s collection exemplified a neoclassical New England style that informed her work, titled Vessel . During her time at the Manufacture, Golann worked with artists on enameling and engraving techniques.

Said’s work, Shaping Time , is a three-tiered vertical sculpture also adorned by relief carvings, as well as piercings and glazed surfaces that draw upon ancient Egyptian and Islamic objects in the Met’s collection. At the Manufacture, Said also worked with the artisans on enameling and engraving, as well as lacquer painting.

Harvey’s Ruined splendour is a bronze diadem composed of forged rhomboid bronze interlaced with panels inspired by the fine filigree seen on ancient Greek necklaces. After creation the work was pierced with rods in order to create its “ruination.” For the work, Harvey drew on ancient jewelry in the Met collection from Greece, India, and China, and then spent time in the Manufacture learning guillochage , a technique for engraving intricate patterns like leaves and flowers onto metal.

In a statement, Met CEO Max Hollein called the program “a collaborative initiative that embodies our mutual commitment to supporting artistic innovation and cultural dialogue.”

article_text:
Salaud Morisset has boarded worldwide sales rights to “Our Way to You” (Ce qui nous mène à toi), the first feature from French-Moroccan filmmaker Khalil Cherti , and produced by Amaury Ovise of Kazak Productions.

While the film already won two awards after its world premiere at this year’s Angoulême Film Festival, it will begin its international tour with the Cairo Intl. Film Festival in November.

The film is distributed in France by Condor Distribution, hitting French theaters on Nov. 11.

The plot delves into Charlie and Hicham’s love story and desire to start a family, as they navigate through the struggle of infertility and assisted reproductive treatment. Over the course of three years, through hope and heartbreak, they will put their love and their bodies to the test.

The cast is led by César award-winning actress Nina Meurisse (“Souleymane’s Story,” 2024; “The Rapture,” 2023) as Charlie, Sofian Khammes (“My Brothers and I,” 2021; “The Big Hit,” 2019) as Hicham, and Jeanne Balibar, who won the Cesar for best actress in 2018 for “Barbara.”

Connection and relationships are recurring themes in Cherti’s work, whether he chooses to relate complicated family bonds (“Wherever Comes the Pain From,” 2013 – selected at Locarno and awarded at Clermont-Ferrand) or the deepness of love in the face of life challenges (“Je, d’un accident ou d’amour,” 2025 – selected at Tribeca and Clermont-Ferrand; “T’embrasser sur le miel,” 2021).

For his first feature film, the director says he wanted to capture one of the most important relationships in a person’s life, as in his opinion, simply being a couple is “an odyssey.”

Cherti added: “I made this film because there is something quietly moving about two people trying, together, through years of hardship, to reinvent themselves.”

Paul Jullien, head of sales at Salaud Morisset, said: “With ‘Our Way to You,’ Khalil Cherti explores the universal themes of parenthood, love and family with remarkable depth and sensitivity, turning an intimate story into something that resonates with us all.”

Amaury Ovise, producer, said the film “sensitively captures the joy and pain of a couple navigating the challenges of assisted reproduction. Charlie and Hicham embody that fragile part of ourselves whose story deserves to be told.”

article_text:
Marco Bassetti , CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, called for European producers to hold their ground when it comes to negotiating terms of trade with the U.S. studios and streamers during a fireside chat at Rome’s MIA market titled “What does it mean today to be a ‘European champion’ in an increasingly competitive global content market?”

“Who invests in creativity? It’s us independent producers,” said Bassetti during the chat with veteran Italian producer Marco Chimenz. He went on to point out that “the major debate currently taking place in Europe — and this is my own personal view — regardless of the different legal systems, across different countries we live under, is about recognizing and providing compensation for creativity,” he added.

Korea Box Office: Anime Feature 'Chiikawa' Edges Past 'The Assassin(s)' to Claim Weekend Crown

The Italian executive went on to point out that “the current battle [in Brussels] over [investment] quotas is instead entirely pointless.” He was referring to contentious rules – known as Europe’s Audiovisual Media Services Directive – that force foreign streaming services to invest a portion of their revenue into local productions, but leaves the modalities of this obligation to each individual country.

But Bassetti sees the rules of engagement as being crucial.

“The real fight should focus on studios and streamers recognizing and providing rewards for creativity” in the form of retention of IP rights on the part of producers, Bassetti added. “Yet that is not what is happening.”

At least not in continental Europe. “But when I work for a TV network — especially in countries like England — I retain ownership of the intellectual property,” he noted. “If I sell a series, the rights eventually revert to me after three years and there’s a built-in incentive for the creator.”

“Here in Europe, we’re accustomed to a system like that,” Bassetti said. “If the streamers just treat production companies as mere service providers it’s a problem,” because you don’t provide an incentive for creators to work with you.

“The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit. There’s some movement regarding ‘windows’ (the sequence of release platforms)—but it’s only a partial shift. Ultimately, they [the studios and the streamers] still have total control,” he said.

Since taking the helm of Stéphane Courbit’s media powerhouse Banijay in 2013, Bassetti has firmly steered the company through some major transformations, from the takeover of production powerhouse Endemol Shine in the thick of the pandemic in 2020 to the diversification of the banner’s activities in live entertainment through Balich Wonder Studio and the Independents, all the while ramping up both scripted and unscripted business, and bolstering new and existing IPs.

It was only two months ago that Banijay Entertainment and RedBird IMI officially completed the $8 billion merger of Banijay and RedBird IMI’s All3Media, which is headquartered in London, U.K. The deal saw All3Media CEO Jane Turton take on the role of deputy CEO of the combined company, which boasts over 265,000 hours of content and some of television’s most recognizable franchises.

While the company is best known for its unscripted IP, thanks to “super brands” like “The Traitors,” “Big Brother” and “MasterChef,” Banijay also makes plenty of top notch scripted TV series and movies such as “Peaky Blinders,” “Black Mirror” and “Hamnet.”

Last week, speaking at the Mipcom TV market in Cannes, Bassetti said he saw an opportunity for the company to grow its presence in scripted production and hinted to an expansion into the U.S. scripted space.

That might help improve terms of trade for Banijay.

Films and events

Galas

Minotaur

Andrey Zvyagintsev transposes Claude Chabrol’s La Femme infidèle to contemporary Russia, delivering a magnificent political allegory that dissects the mechanics of ego, violence and corruption.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Screening at cinemas around the UK – find out more .

Credits

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev

Screenwriters Simon Lyashenko, Andrey Zvyagintsev

With Dmitriy Mazurov, Iris Lebedeva, Boris Kudrin, Yuriy Zavalnyouk, Varvara Zmykova

France-Germany-Latvia 2026. 141min

Courtesy of MUBI

Language Russian With English subtitles

Certificate LFF18

Access information

Friday 16 October 17:45

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Saturday 17 October 20:00

Descriptive subtitles

Sunday 18 October 20:00

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

At the onset of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Gleb, a powerful CEO, is preoccupied with feeding the war machine with workers, when he learns of his wife’s infidelity. Faced with this discovery and a complex professional decision, his scruples quickly fade. Zvyagintsev’s masterful and darkly humorous tale of impunity will make your blood run cold.

Diana Cipriano

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury, nudity, and sex.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Mariinka

Shot over ten years, this unflinching portrait of youth in Eastern Ukraine is a rare and powerful account of the passing of time during conflict.

Imperium

Master of archival film reconstruction, Sergei Loznitsa, reframes Soviet history once again via the revealing gaze of Italian cameramen who captured life there in the early 1970s.

Fjord

This searching, Palme d’Or-winning moral dilemma pits preaching conservative Christian parents against a holier-than-thou liberal system.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 随着巴顿庄园（Button House）的幽灵们携一部关于出逃幽灵的情节登上大银幕，我们了解到这个团队只是太舍不得彼此——以及为什么哼哧作响的罗宾（Robin）可能会拥有自己的剧集。当《鬼屋欢乐送》的最后一集于2023年12月播出时，这部情景喜剧感觉像是迎来了……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "当《鬼屋欢乐送》的最后一集于2023年12月播出时，这部情景喜剧感觉像是迎来了尘埃落定的结局。由夏洛特·里奇（Charlotte Ritchie）饰演的艾莉森（Alison）与那些游荡在她继承的破败庄园里的幽灵之间核心关系，在他们鼓励她将庄园卖给酒店开发商时得到了整洁的收尾。对于数百万观看该剧的观众，以及幕后的演员和剧组成员来说，这都是一集催人泪下的剧集。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们当时停拍这部剧时，真的完全没有要回来的打算，”该剧共同主创马修·拜恩顿（Mathew Baynton）解释道，他在剧中饰演涉世未深且满脑子浪漫情怀的诗人托马斯（Thomas）。他现在正坐在一间伦敦酒店套房的贵妃椅边缘，那个位置坐着并不舒服，他接着说道：“我们在拍摄的最后一天都哭了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“它完结时我太难过了，”在贵妃椅另一头坐得更板正的洛莉·阿德福普（Lolly Adefope）补充道，她在剧中饰演兴奋过头的基蒂（Kitty）。“那种感觉就像你在派对上，而你们要走了。”", "links": [{"text": "Lolly Adefope", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2024/mar/31/nothing-beats-making-your-friends-laugh-lolly-adefope-on-the-absurdity-of-fame-the-trouble-with-netflix-and-saying-goodbye-to-ghosts"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这是一个清晰的结局，大家觉得他们已经充分挖掘了所有角色，”导演西蒙·海恩德（Simon Hynd)说道，“但我确实注意到他们其中一些人的眼中闪过一丝遗憾。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "简而言之，《鬼屋欢乐送》现在又回来了。尽管电视剧系列已经结束，但故事将在新电影《Ghosts: The Possession of Button House》中继续。所以问题是，究竟是谁先眨了眼？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们在 Monumental 的高管艾莉森·卡彭特（Alison Carpenter）开始说：‘如果你们想做的话，我们可以为一部电影拉到资金，’”拜恩顿解释说。“但我们当时只是把这个提议给挡了回去。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当时的担心是，你最后拍出来的会是一集90分钟的电视剧，感觉就像是《Please Sir! The Movie》一样，”共同主创兼主演劳伦斯·里卡德（Laurence Rickard）说道，他在剧中同时饰演山顶洞人罗宾和被斩首的贵族亨弗雷·博恩爵士（Sir Humphrey Bone）。“顺便说一句，我很喜欢那部片子。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最终，卡彭特说服了该剧的六位主创兼主演（其余几位是西蒙·法纳比（Simon Farnaby）、玛莎·豪-道格拉斯（Martha Howe-Douglas）、吉姆·霍威克（Jim Howick）和本·威尔邦德（Ben Willbond），他们未出席）至少坐进一个房间里讨论这个可能性。“我们把大家都不希望它变成什么样，以及为了成为一部电影它必须是什么样，全都讨论了一遍，”拜恩顿解释道。“这很快就把我们引向了‘附身’这个概念，它能让其中一个幽灵离开这片庭院。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这是史上节奏最快的一次转折，”里卡德笑着说。“我们早上9:30进去的时候还在想：‘我的意思是，能见到大家挺好的，但我觉着答案大概是“不”’——然后到了11点，我们就变成了：‘我们必须得拍这个。’\"", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最终呈现的电影依然非常具有《鬼屋欢乐送》的特色，既有其独特的尖锐荒诞感（比如某个时刻，一块占卜板拼出了“离开”来表达对英国脱欧的看法），又有近乎折磨人的感人情感（你可能再也无法在不哭泣的情况下看苏格兰蛋了）。但它毫无疑问是一部电影，有着悬念、倒计时和宏大的场景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“附身的想法立刻让人联想起灵魂互换之类的东西，这让我们想到了《飞越未来》（Big），”拜恩顿说。“然后我们在讨论，如果附身没有持续下去而他的灵魂正在消逝会怎么样，这让我们想到了《回到未来》（Back to the Future）。那群闯入房子的孩子们感觉就像《七宝奇谋》（The Goonies）。我们对于这部电影的所有参考点，都是我们在年轻时喜爱的电影。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影是一个令人惊叹的壮举，不仅因为它的筹备周期极短——海恩德直到去年年底才得知这部电影的消息——还因为其全员阵容中的每一位成员都在情节中扮演着至关重要的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在拍剧集时，我们已经习惯了编写多线叙事，”拜恩顿解释道。“在任何一集里，实际的故事都是通过两三个短暂的时刻讲完的，所以这无论如何已经成了我们的写作模式。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/31916e79fb05882764c737ec8b40b6fcdba74675/33_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "洛莉·阿德福普饰演的基蒂·海厄姆（Kitty Higham）身穿华丽的历史服饰和羽毛头饰，透过门口凝视着外面", "caption": "‘我是演员阵容里最 Z 世代的成员’……洛莉·阿德福普在片中。摄影：Mandozzi Photography/PA", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种方法意味着，尽管不再住在巴顿庄园，由基尔·史密斯-拜诺（Kiell Smith-Bynoe）饰演的艾莉森和她的丈夫迈克（Mike）发现自己也被卷入了行动之中。史密斯-拜诺对自己的角色弧光似乎尤为满意。“迈克在这一部里得以证明了自己，”他解释说，“在度过了好几年没能做到这一点的时光之后，这感觉很不错。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "可以说，史密斯-拜诺在《鬼屋欢乐送》中一直承担着最艰难的表演工作，因为迈克通常是屏幕上唯一一个不是幽灵、也无法与他们互动的人。在电影的高潮部分，这种挑战加倍了——在不剧透太多的前提下，满满一屋子的新老角色在实体化与虚无之间进进出出。“我花了一会儿才适应，”他说。“我不得不一直问西蒙我应该能够看到谁。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一次的大部分演员都是新面孔，也就是前面提到的那些孩子们。要想从像这样才华横溢的演员阵容手中抢走一部电影的风头绝非易事，但在《我发誓》（I Swear）中饰演年轻约翰·戴维森（John Davidson）的斯科特·埃利斯·沃森（Scott Ellis Watson）在这里表现得极为惊艳，这在很大程度上是因为他花了很多时间完美模仿了一个已故的中年保守党议员。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些新加入的演员是阿德福普格外欣赏的。“身边有斯科特陪伴太有趣了，”她说。“我算是演员阵容里最 Z 世代的成员，所以我们经常聊迷因（meme）和 TikTok。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“你当时是儿童密语者，对吧？”里卡德说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“是的，没错。我在为你们翻译，”她笑着回应道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在电视剧中，这六位创作者可以分头行动，由他们剧团的各种组合形式来编写不同的剧集。但这部电影署名归所有六个人。这做起来难吗？“这只是一个看谁在什么时间有空的过程，”贝恩顿说，“所以有时是我们两个人，有时是三四个。最棒的一点是，那个暂时缺席的人在回来时就会成为你们的‘新鲜视角’。有时你会陷入一种地步，满眼只看到A方案或B方案，而这两个方案都存在问题，但这时一个已经离开几周的人走进来会说：‘那C方案呢？’然后你会说：‘哦，对啊！’\"", article_text:
W hen the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.

“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.

“I was so upset that it finished,” adds Lolly Adefope , who plays the excitable Kitty, from the better structured end of the chaise. “It was like being at a party and you guys were leaving.”

“It was a clear ending, and the guys felt like they had fully explored all of the characters,” says director Simon Hynd, “but I did notice a look of regret in some of their eyes.”

All of which is to say that Ghosts is now back. Although the television series remains over, the story will continue in the new film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House. So the question is, who blinked first?

“Alison Carpenter, our executive at Monumental, had started to say, ‘We could get the funding for a film if you guys want to do that,’” explains Baynton. “But we just batted it away.”

“The fear was that you’d end up making a 90-minute episode of a TV show, and it would feel like, Please Sir! The Movie,” says co-creator and star Laurence Rickard, who plays both caveman Robin and decapitated nobleman Sir Humphrey Bone. “Which I love, by the way.”

Eventually Carpenter convinced the show’s six creators and stars (the others being Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond, not present) to at least get into a room and discuss the prospect. “We all talked through what we didn’t want it to be, and what it sort of had to be to be a film,” explains Baynton. “That led us very quickly to the concept of possession, which would allow one of the ghosts to get out of the grounds.”

“It was the fastest turnaround ever,” laughs Rickard. “We went in at 9:30am going ‘I mean, it’s nice to see everyone, but I think the answer is probably no’ – and then by 11 o’clock, we were going, ‘We have to do this.’”

The resulting film is still very much Ghosts, with its unique mix of sharp absurdity (at one point a Ouija board spells out ‘Leave’ to make a point about Brexit) and near-debilitating emotional notes (you may never again look at a scotch egg without crying). But it is undoubtedly a movie, with stakes and a ticking clock and big set pieces.

“The possession idea immediately invites a body swap sort of thing, which reminded us of Big,” says Baynton. “Then we were talking about, what if the possession doesn’t last and his spirit is fading, which reminded us of Back to the Future. The group of kids breaking into the house felt like The Goonies. All our touchstones for this were films we loved in our youth.”

The film is an astonishing feat, not just because of its quick turnaround – Hynd only learned of the film late last year – but because every member of its ensemble has a vital part to play in the plot.

“With the series, we got so used to writing multi-thread narratives,” explains Baynton. “In any episode, the actual stories are told in two or three brief moments, so that had become our mode of writing anyway.”

This approach meant that, despite no longer living in Button House, Alison and her husband Mike, played by Kiell Smith-Bynoe, find themselves swept up in the action. Smith-Bynoe seems especially pleased with his arc. “Mike gets to prove himself in this one,” he explains, “which felt good after spending a few years not getting to do that.”

Smith-Bynoe has arguably always had the hardest acting job on Ghosts, as Mike is often the only person on screen who isn’t a ghost and can’t interact with them. This challenge was doubled for the film’s climax when, without giving too much away, a roomful of characters old and new flit in and out of tangibility. “It took me a minute,” he says. “I had to keep asking Simon who I was supposed to be able to see.”

Much of the cast this time around are new, in the form of the aforementioned kids. It takes a lot to steal a film out from underneath a cast as talented as this, but Scott Ellis Watson, who played the young John Davidson in I Swear, is phenomenal here, largely because he spends a lot of time doing a bang-on impersonation of a dead middle-aged Tory MP.

The new additions were something that Adefope in particular appreciated. “It was so fun having Scott around,” she says. “I was sort of the Gen Z member of the cast, so we talked a lot about memes and TikTok.”

“You were the child whisperer, weren’t you?” says Rickard.

“Yes, exactly. I was translating for you,” she smiles back.

With the show, the six creators were able to break off and write individual episodes in various permutations of their troupe. But the film is credited to all six of them. Was that a hard thing to accomplish? “It was just a process of who was around at what time,” says Baynton. “So sometimes it was two of us, sometimes three or four. What is lovely about that is that the person who’s absent for a little period of time then becomes your fresh pair of eyes when they return. You get to a point at times where all you can see is A or B and both of them are problematic, but then someone who’s been away for a couple of weeks comes in and goes, ‘Well, what about C?’ And you go, ‘Oh yeah!’”

A lot of this is simply muscle memory. The Ghosts team are now veterans, having met while making the Horrible Histories TV show almost two decades ago, and continued with the sitcom Yonderland and the 2015 Shakespeare comedy film Bill. It’s hard to think of any writing and performing group this large who have managed to stay intact for so long. Even Monty Python ran out of films and shows in less time, their work together now largely consisting of tweeting hatred at each other.

“Oh, we’ve got that phase to look forward to,” laughs Rickard. “I’ve been drafting some of that stuff.”

Rickard is the one who seems to have most keenly felt the absence of Ghosts: “The first year after the series stopped was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years.” You get the sense that this film exists in part because its creators missed hanging out with each other.

So why stop the party now? Will there be anything else to look forward to from the gang? “There isn’t something secretly being developed,” insists Baynton. “But we’ve always had the same feeling, which is that we love working together and we’ll keep doing it if people will pay us to do it.”

Does that mean more Ghosts films? That prompts a slightly more uneasy response. “This does sort of feel like, you know, the big swan song,” replies Rickard.

“Yes, but we said that before, so no one can take our word for it,” adds Baynton. “But there’s no intention. Also, ghosts can’t age, and I’m rapidly getting way too old to play Thomas.”

“But Robin could definitely have a spinoff, and that wouldn’t be a problem,” cracks Rickard, noting that he’s looking more and more like a long-dead caveman with every passing year. “It would be great. My makeup call would get shaved right down.”

Ava DuVernay’s timely and viscerally moving “ 14th ” leads this year’s Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations with six, including best documentary feature. Close behind with five nominations apiece are Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s examination of Elizabeth Holmes, “ You Can See Everything ”; Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman’s polar bear migration story, “Nuisance Bear”; David Greaves’ archival portrait of Black cultural history, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and Pegah Ahangarani’s Iranian historical documentary, “Rehearsals for a Revolution.”

Netflix led all distributors with 17 nominations, nearly double the nine earned by runner-up Neon.

DuVernay, Fielder and Oppenheim are among the directing nominees, alongside Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor for “NAZA,” Felipe Bustos Sierra for “Everybody to Kenmure Street,” Ross McElwee for “Remake” and Orlando von Einsiedel for “The Cycle of Love,” the only directing nominee whose film did not land a documentary feature nom.

Now in its 11th year, the Critics Choice Documentary Awards will take place Nov. 8 at the Edison Ballroom in New York City, with television host and producer Ross Matthews serving as host. The awards celebrate excellence in nonfiction filmmaking.

The organization’s track record of predicting Oscar success has been mixed over the years. Its inaugural top prize winner, “O.J.: Made in America” (2016), went on to win the Academy Award for documentary feature. Since then, only three other top prize winners or nominees have crossed over to the Oscars: winner “Summer of Soul (…Or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised)” (2021) and nominees “Will & Harper” (2024) and last year’s “The Perfect Neighbor” (2025). All others failed to be nominated, or in some cases, not even make the preliminary shortlist (i.e., 2022’s “Good Night Oppy”).

As previously announced, Ron Howard will receive the Critics Choice Impact Award. Visionary filmmaker Jehane Noujaim will receive the CCA’s Pennebaker Award, presented by Chris Hegedus, Pennebaker’s widow and longtime collaborator. Named in honor of trailblazing documentarian D.A. Pennebaker, the award, formerly known as the Critics Choice Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizes filmmakers whose careers have made a profound and lasting contribution to documentary storytelling.

Feature-length documentaries, two-part documentaries and short-form documentaries are eligible for nomination if they were first released commercially in the U.S. between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2026.
